flagged.evidence: It displays alpha^op as an arrow from ((X⊗Y)⊗Z) to X⊗(Y⊗Z), while saying it is obtained by viewing the original alpha in the opposite category. But def-opposite-category states C^op(A,B)=C(B,A): the original alpha in that direction becomes an arrow X⊗(Y⊗Z) to ((X⊗Y)⊗Z) in C^op. The displayed standard-direction associator must instead be the opposite of alpha inverse; likewise the unitors require opposite inverses. The written structure maps therefore do not type-check.

The definition calls both F2 and the single map F0: 1'→F(1) “natural transformations,” then says that F0 is a “natural isomorphism.” Its cited dependency def-natural-isomorphism defines one as a natural transformation alpha:F⇒G, i.e. a family of components indexed by a source category. F0 is one morphism between two objects, not such a family; it should be required to be an isomorphism, not a natural isomorphism.

Step 1.1 says “* has the same unit because” lambda(1⊗1)lambda^-1=1. This proves only 1*1=1, not 1*f=f=f*1 for arbitrary f. The cited thm-eckmann-hilton-argument requires two unital operations with the same unit, and def-semigroup-and-monoid defines a unit as two-sided for every element. Thus the hypothesis of [L3] has not been established when step 3.1 invokes it. Naturality of both unitors plus their equality on the tensor unit could repair the gap, but neither calculation is supplied here.

The Example says “The five parenthesised tensor words on four letters are” and step 2.1 calls the list complete. But def-parenthesised-tensor-word permits the unit symbol as a word, so ((A⊗1)⊗(B⊗(C⊗D))) is another valid word on the ordered letters A,B,C,D. The cited Catalan theorem expressly counts only words “with no inserted unit symbol,” a restriction missing from the Example. Hence the asserted complete list is false under the page’s own definition.
